# Bookmuse

> Bookmuse is a book-summaries app for iPhone, iPad and Android: big ideas from great books, made visual. Each summary is a short course of interactive lessons (diagrams that move, guess-first questions, a quiz and the key takeaways) that teaches a book's core ideas in a few short sittings.

Bookmuse is free to download. One summary a day is free to read in full, the same one for everyone (it changes at 00:00 UTC); every other summary opens as a preview (the intro and the first three lessons). Bookmuse Pro, a monthly or yearly subscription in the App Store (the yearly plan starts with a 7-day free trial), opens every summary and adds 10 GB of cloud storage and more Bookmuse AI. Reading summaries needs a free account. The app needs iOS or iPadOS 26 and also runs on Apple-silicon Macs as the iPad app. Summaries are in English. It was made by Quan Ngo Van (wanngo).

## How a summary works

- An intro: the book's core idea in one or two sentences, a little about the author, and the list of lessons.
- Five to eight lessons, one big idea each, two or three minutes each. Lessons explain with short text, diagrams, charts and maps, animations, guess-first questions (answer before you are told), quick checks, small things to try (sliders, drag-to-explore charts) and everyday examples.
- A quiz that checks the ideas and explains the answers.
- The key takeaways on one screen.
- One lesson on screen at a time, with a bar that shows where you are; your place syncs across devices.
- Anyone can try a summary in a web browser from its share link; today's free summary is always at https://bookmuse-app.wanngo.com/s/today

## Books

- Popular non-fiction across self-growth, productivity, happiness, business and career, money and investing, leadership, negotiation, relationships, health, society and tech, personalities and spirituality, among others. New summaries are added every week.
- Shelves on Home: Free Today, Picked for You (from the interests you choose and what you read), Because you read…, collections, Popular, New and categories.
- Ratings and reviews from other readers on each summary.

## Lessons made by your AI

- Connect an AI agent (Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, Claude Code) to your Bookmuse library through the Bookmuse MCP server and ask it for a lesson on any topic. It adds an interactive HTML lesson to your Library, with its diagrams and quizzes working.
- Agents manage the person's own books, highlights, saved words and folders. They can't read summaries, post to the feed or make share links.

## Your own books, too

- Open DRM-free EPUB, PDF, Kindle (MOBI, AZW3), FB2, TXT and Markdown files, HTML notes and comics (CBZ, CBR) from Files, Google Drive, Dropbox or catalogs such as Project Gutenberg.
- Free on-device voices read them aloud in English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese, Vietnamese, Chinese and Japanese.
- Bookmuse AI explains a word in its sentence and answers questions about the page.
- A web dashboard at https://bookmuse-app.wanngo.com manages your own books from a computer: upload, edit details and covers, folders, download and delete.

## Every summary in full detail

### Thinking, Fast and Slow — Daniel Kahneman
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/thinking-fast-and-slow/
Core idea: Your mind runs on a fast, automatic storyteller that feels sure and a slow, lazy checker that mostly signs off, so thinking better means learning the storyteller's tricks by name and slowing down when the stakes are high.
About the book: Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011) is Daniel Kahneman's tour of how the mind makes judgments and choices. Kahneman, a psychologist who won the Nobel Prize in economics, spent decades testing how people really think, much of it with his friend Amos Tversky. The book describes two ways of thinking, a fast one that jumps to a story and a slow one that is supposed to check it, and the mistakes that come from trusting the fast one too much. It is for anyone who wants to spot those mistakes in their own decisions.
Categories: Productivity, Self-Growth
Length: 8 lessons, 18 min
Lessons:
1. Two characters in your head: The fast mind that answers, and the lazy one that checks
2. What you see is all there is: A confident story from little, and an easy swap
3. Anchors pull your guess: A number you just saw drags your answer, and two shortcuts like it
4. Luck in a skill costume: Why results fall back, and why the past looks obvious
5. When to trust your gut: Formulas, and the two conditions for real expertise
6. Plan with the outside view: Why plans run late, and how to check them
7. Losses loom larger: Prospect theory, ownership and framing
8. Two selves: The self that lives and the self that remembers

### Atomic Habits — James Clear
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/atomic-habits/
Core idea: Small habits, repeated every day, build the person you want to become. Make good habits obvious, attractive, easy and satisfying, and flip those four laws to break bad ones.
About the book: Atomic Habits (2018) is James Clear's practical guide to building good habits and breaking bad ones. Clear, a writer who rebuilt his own life with small habits after a serious injury in high school, draws on psychology and everyday stories. He argues that results come from systems, not goals: tiny changes, repeated every day, add up to big ones. The book gives four simple laws that make any habit easier to start and harder to drop.
Categories: Self-Growth, Productivity
Length: 7 lessons, 17 min
Lessons:
1. Tiny gains add up: Get 1% better each day, and trust your system
2. Habits shape who you are: Every action is a vote for who you become
3. The habit loop: Four steps, four laws, and how to flip them
4. The first law: make it obvious: Give a habit a clear cue. To break one: make it invisible
5. The second law: make it attractive: Pair it with something you want. To break one: make it unattractive
6. The third law: make it easy: Start in two minutes. To break a habit: make it difficult
7. The fourth law: make it satisfying: Reward it right away. To break a habit: make it unsatisfying

### How to Read a Book — Mortimer J. Adler
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/how-to-read-a-book/
Core idea: A hard book can lift your understanding, but only if you work on it: first to see its shape, then to grasp what it says, and last to judge it fairly.
About the book: How to Read a Book is a guide to reading for understanding, first published in 1940 by the American philosopher Mortimer J. Adler. It says that a book above your level can lift you only if you read it actively, in three ways: for its structure, for its meaning and for a fair judgment. Adler gives rules for practicing on the great books, and he ends by arguing that readers who can do this become free minds. It is for anyone who can read but wants to read better.
Categories: Productivity, Self-Growth
Length: 7 lessons, 20 min
Lessons:
1. Read to understand more: Facts alone leave you where you stood
2. Three readings, one habit: The whole list of rules, and how practice joins them
3. See the skeleton: What kind of book, what it says, how it fits
4. Come to terms: Use the key words in the author's sense
5. Say it in your own words: Claims, arguments and two tests of understanding
6. Talk back, fairly: Judge only after you understand, and give reasons
7. Start with the great books: Learn on books that teach, and read them together

### The Mountain Is You — Brianna Wiest
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/the-mountain-is-you/
Core idea: Self-sabotage is not a flaw. It is a way of coping that meets a need you cannot see, so you get free by finding the need, feeling what you avoid, and changing one small step at a time.
About the book: The Mountain Is You is a 2020 book by the writer Brianna Wiest about self-sabotage. She argues that the habits that hold us back are not signs of weakness. They are ways of coping that meet needs we do not see. The book is for anyone who keeps getting in their own way, and it shows how to understand those needs, feel what is underneath, and build a new life one small step at a time.
Categories: Self-Growth, Happiness
Length: 7 lessons, 17 min
Lessons:
1. Self-sabotage is a need in disguise: Why you cannot stop a habit you hate, and what it protects.
2. Comfort pulls you back: Why a change for the better can feel wrong at first.
3. Your feelings are messages: What anger, jealousy and regret are pointing at.
4. Worry is not protection: Why worry grows, and how to end a fear.
5. Small steps change you: How tiny daily actions beat big breakthroughs.
6. Let go by building: How to leave a painful past behind.
7. Choose how you respond: Why your power lies in what you do, not what you feel.

### Being Mortal — Atul Gawande
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/being-mortal/
Core idea: When a body can no longer be fixed, safety and a longer life are not enough: people want to stay the authors of their own story, so doctors, care homes and families must ask what matters most and shape care around it.
About the book: Being Mortal (2014) is surgeon Atul Gawande's book about aging, serious illness and dying. He was never taught about mortality in medical school, and he uses patients, his wife's grandmother and his own father to show how medicine, nursing homes and families treat the last chapters of life. He argues that modern medicine is good at fixing and prolonging life but poor at helping people live well when they cannot be fixed. It is for anyone who will face aging or illness, their own or a parent's.
Categories: Health, Spirituality
Length: 8 lessons, 20 min
Lessons:
1. When independence ends: We prize living alone, but that ends, and few plan for it.
2. Managing decline: Old age is wearing down, and good care protects what matters.
3. Homes built for safety: Nursing homes began as a fix for hospitals, not a life for people.
4. A home, not a ward: Help works best in your own home, on your terms.
5. A reason to live: Something to care for, and the right to write your own story.
6. Hope is not a plan: Why we chase more treatment, and what hospice and talking change.
7. The hard conversation: The questions that turn a doctor into a guide.
8. Two kinds of courage: Face the truth, then act on it, and shape the ending.

### The Monk Who Sold His Ferrari — Robin Sharma
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/the-monk-who-sold-his-ferrari/
Core idea: A fulfilling life is built from the inside: a trained mind, a clear purpose, daily self-improvement and a life of giving, lived now and not later.
About the book: The Monk Who Sold His Ferrari is a fable by Robin Sharma, a former lawyer, first published in 1997. A star trial lawyer sells his mansion and his Ferrari after a heart attack, and learns seven virtues from sages in the Himalayas. It argues that a fulfilling life is built from the inside, and it offers simple daily practices. It is a story, not research, for readers who feel busy and empty.
Categories: Happiness, Self-Growth
Length: 7 lessons, 18 min
Lessons:
1. Master your mind: The garden: what you let into your mind decides what grows.
2. Follow your purpose: The lighthouse: know what you want and aim at it.
3. Practice kaizen: The sumo wrestler: improve yourself a little every day.
4. Live with discipline: The pink wire cable: build willpower from small acts.
5. Respect your time: The gold stopwatch: spend it on what counts.
6. Selflessly serve others: The yellow roses: your life is only as good as what you give.
7. Embrace the present: The path of diamonds: do not put off living.

### Can't Hurt Me — David Goggins
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/can-t-hurt-me/
Core idea: Most people quit long before their limit, and you can move that limit by telling yourself the truth, doing hard things on purpose and learning from every failure.
About the book: Can't Hurt Me is a 2018 book by David Goggins, a retired Navy SEAL. He tells how he went from a poor, abused childhood and a night job killing pests to SEAL training and some of the hardest races in the world. He argues that most people stop long before their limit, and that a mind toughened by hard things can go much further. Ten chapters end with a challenge for the reader.
Categories: Self-Growth, Leadership
Length: 7 lessons, 19 min
Lessons:
1. Tell yourself the truth: Say what is really true, then put small goals on a mirror
2. Walk toward discomfort: Do something hard on purpose, then do it again
3. A calloused mind: Hard times can toughen you, if you choose to see them that way
4. The Cookie Jar: Use your past wins to keep going when you want to quit
5. The 40% Rule: When you feel done, you have more left, so go a little further
6. Prepare for the pain: Picture the win and the trouble, then train for both
7. Fail, then learn: Take every failure apart, fix it, and try again

### The Prince — Niccolò Machiavelli
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/the-prince/
Core idea: A ruler keeps power by judging people as they really are, relying on his own strength, never making his people hate him, and preparing in calm times for the day luck turns.
About the book: The Prince is a short book of advice to a ruler, written by Niccolò Machiavelli as a gift for Lorenzo de’ Medici. It argues that a ruler should judge people as they are, rely on his own strength, avoid being hated, and prepare for bad luck. The advice is harsh, and the book admits that some of the means it describes bring power but no glory.
Categories: Personalities, Leadership
Length: 7 lessons, 16 min
Lessons:
1. See people as they are: Plan for how people really act, not for how they should.
2. Fear is safer than love: Love breaks when interest calls. Fear holds.
3. Never be hated or despised: The best protection is the good will of your people.
4. The lion and the fox: A ruler needs force and cunning, and must look good.
5. Your own arms: Hired and lent soldiers fail you. Build your own.
6. Hurt once, help slowly: Do the harm you must at once. Give benefits a little at a time.
7. Luck is only half: Use calm times to prepare for the flood.

### How to Talk to Anyone — Leil Lowndes
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/how-to-talk-to-anyone/
Core idea: Success with people comes from small moves you can learn, and every one of them aims at the same thing: making the other person feel special and at ease.
About the book: How to Talk to Anyone is a guide to ninety-two small tricks for meeting people, talking with them and winning their trust. Leil Lowndes, a communications coach, wrote it, and this edition was first published in 1999. She read the research on how people connect and watched very successful, well-liked people to find what they do. She argues that these moves can be learned, and the book is for anyone who wants easier conversations at work, at parties and on the phone.
Categories: Negotiation
Length: 8 lessons, 16 min
Lessons:
1. Your body speaks first: A slow smile and steady eyes make people feel special
2. Small talk is music: Match their mood, then say almost anything with warmth
3. Put the spotlight on them: Ask, listen and remember, and they enjoy you
4. Learn a little of their world: A few opening questions open any crowd
5. Use their words: People trust people who seem like them
6. Praise people believe: Specific and personal, not a favor in disguise
7. Smile in your voice: On the phone, say out loud what your face would show
8. Never put people on the spot: Keep tough talk and small slips out of the moment

### The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People — Stephen R. Covey
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/the-7-habits-of-highly-effective-people/
Core idea: Lasting change works from the inside out: change how you see things, then build seven habits that take you from depending on others, to standing on your own, to working well with others.
About the book: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People is a self-help classic by Stephen R. Covey, first published in 1989. Covey read about 200 years of writing on success and found that the early books taught character, while later ones taught image and quick tricks. He argues that lasting change works from the inside out: you change how you see things, then build seven habits that move you from depending on others, to standing on your own, to working well with others. A habit of regular renewal keeps it all going.
Categories: Self-Growth, Productivity, Leadership
Length: 8 lessons, 19 min
Lessons:
1. See it from the inside out: Why tricks fail, and the map of all seven habits
2. Habit 1: Be proactive: Between what happens and what you do, you get to choose
3. Habit 2: Begin with the end in mind: Know where you are going before you climb
4. Habit 3: Put first things first: Spend your time on what matters, not on what shouts
5. Habit 4: Think win/win: Look for answers where everyone gains
6. Habit 5: Seek first to understand: Listen to understand, then ask to be understood
7. Habit 6: Synergize: Treat differences as the way to a better answer
8. Habit 7: Sharpen the saw: Renew body, mind, heart and spirit so the other habits last

### The Psychology of Money — Morgan Housel
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/the-psychology-of-money/
Core idea: How you behave with money matters much more than how much you know about it.
About the book: The Psychology of Money is a 2020 book by writer Morgan Housel. It uses short stories to argue that how you behave with money matters more than how much you know. In twenty short chapters it covers luck, risk, saving, time and the price of investing, for anyone who wants to feel calmer about money.
Categories: Money & Investments, Business & Career
Length: 8 lessons, 20 min
Lessons:
1. No one is crazy: Your own life shapes how you see money, so odd choices can make sense.
2. Luck and risk are twins: Success is never as great, and failure never as awful, as it looks.
3. Know when you have enough: Wanting more than enough makes rich people risk everything.
4. Time does the work: Staying in the game for decades beats the biggest return.
5. Leave room for error: Plan for your plan to go wrong.
6. A few things drive everything: Half your picks can fail and you can still win.
7. Wealth is what you don't see: Money you do not spend buys control of your time.
8. Pay the price of returns: See market drops as a fee, not a fine.

### The ONE Thing — Gary Keller, Jay Papasan
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/the-one-thing/
Core idea: Big results come from going small: find the ONE Thing that makes everything else easier or unnecessary, and do it first.
About the book: The ONE Thing is a 2013 book by Gary Keller, the cofounder of Keller Williams Realty, with writer Jay Papasan. It argues that big results come from going small: doing one right thing at a time, like falling dominoes. The book names six lies about success, then gives one question for finding what matters most and a plan for protecting the time to act on it. It is for anyone who feels busy and behind.
Categories: Productivity
Length: 7 lessons, 16 min
Lessons:
1. One domino at a time: Why one right action can start a chain of results
2. Six lies about success: The beliefs that pull you off course, and the truth for each
3. Find the vital few: Cut a long list down until one thing is left
4. The Focusing Question: One question that shows your first domino
5. From purpose to right now: Turn a big goal into the next thing to do
6. Time block your ONE Thing: Give it the best hours of your day, and guard them
7. Guard it from four thieves: What steals your focus, and how to stop it

### The Body Keeps the Score — Bessel van der Kolk
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/the-body-keeps-the-score/
Core idea: Trauma is not only what happened. It is the mark left on the brain and body, and healing means helping them feel safe in the present.
About the book: The Body Keeps the Score is a 2014 book by the psychiatrist Bessel van der Kolk about how trauma changes the brain and body. He draws on forty years of work with veterans and with adults and children hurt in childhood. He argues that trauma is not only a past event but a mark that keeps the body's alarm switched on, so healing needs the body, other people and more than talk.
Categories: Happiness
Length: 8 lessons, 21 min
Lessons:
1. Trauma is a mark, not a memory: Why the war did not end for a veteran named Tom
2. The alarm that will not switch off: What brain scans show during a flashback
3. Losing touch with your body: Numbness, and why feeling your body comes first
4. We calm each other down: Safety is shared, from a baby's first days onward
5. Childhood wounds are common and hidden: A large study, and why labels miss the cause
6. Trauma is remembered in pieces: Why a clear story may not be enough
7. Healing starts in the body: Six ways to calm the alarm, and a yoga study
8. Many roads back: Three roads to healing, and how to choose help

### The Power of Habit — Charles Duhigg
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/the-power-of-habit/
Core idea: Habits are loops that run without thought, and once you know how a loop works, you can change it.
About the book: The Power of Habit (2012) is journalist Charles Duhigg's look at the science of habits. It explains how a habit works in the brain, why some stick, and how to change them, in people, companies and whole societies. It argues that habits can be changed once we understand their parts. It is for anyone who wants to build a routine or drop one.
Categories: Productivity, Self-Growth
Length: 8 lessons, 20 min
Lessons:
1. Every habit is a loop: Cue, routine and reward
2. A craving drives the loop: Why a cue and a reward are not enough
3. Keep the cue, change the routine: The Golden Rule of habit change, in four steps
4. Belief grows in a group: What holds a new routine under stress
5. One habit can change the rest: Keystone habits and small wins
6. Willpower becomes a habit: Why willpower tires, and a plan for hard moments
7. How a movement is built: Friends, community and new habits
8. You can choose your habits: Why knowing a habit makes it yours

### Boundaries — Dr. Henry Cloud, Dr. John Townsend
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/boundaries/
Core idea: A boundary is the property line of your life: it shows what you own and what is someone else’s, and setting it clearly lets you give a real yes and a real no instead of giving out of fear or guilt.
About the book: Boundaries (1992) is a self-help book by Henry Cloud and John Townsend, two licensed psychologists who write from a Christian view. It argues that a boundary is the property line of your life, showing what you own and what you do not. The authors explain how boundaries go wrong, how they grow, and how to set them with family, friends, a spouse, children and work. Their aim is not to make you less loving, but to help you love freely instead of out of fear or guilt.
Categories: Self-Growth, Love & Sex
Length: 7 lessons, 20 min
Lessons:
1. Your yard and mine: A boundary shows what is yours to own, and what is not
2. Four ways boundaries go wrong: Can’t say no, can’t hear no, and their two twins
3. Bond first, then say no: Safe love comes before limits, for children and for you
4. Let choices have consequences: Why nagging and rescuing fail, and what a limit says
5. When to say yes: A yes you can’t mean is not love, and boundaries are not selfish
6. How to say no and hold it: Say it kindly, feel for them, and expect pushback
7. Growing boundaries, step by step: Eleven signs that show how far you have come

### Cosmos — Carl Sagan
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/cosmos/
Core idea: We live on a small world in a vast and ancient Cosmos, we come from it, and science is how we found out.
About the book: Cosmos is a 1980 book by the astronomer Carl Sagan, written beside his thirteen-part television series. It tells how people learned the size, the age and the makeup of the universe, from a stick and a shadow in ancient Alexandria to spacecraft that left Earth. It argues that we are a small part of a vast Cosmos, that science is how we found this out, and that our survival depends on keeping that wider view.
Categories: Society & Tech
Length: 10 lessons, 25 min
Lessons:
1. A small place in a vast Cosmos: Earth is one rare spot in a mostly empty universe.
2. A world that can be understood: A stick, a shadow and a good question measured the Earth.
3. Facts beat a favorite idea: Kepler gave up the circle because of eight small minutes.
4. Venus is a warning: A twin of Earth became a furnace, so care for ours.
5. How selection builds life: A crab with a samurai face shows how life is shaped.
6. We are made of starstuff: The atoms in you were made inside stars.
7. To look far is to look back: Distant light shows the past, and the universe's start.
8. Memory beyond the body: Genes, brains and libraries, and what a lost library costs.
9. Are we alone?: Seven guesses, and one that decides the answer.
10. Who speaks for Earth?: One species on one fragile world.

### Crucial Conversations — Joseph Grenny, Kerry Patterson, Ron McMillan, Al Switzler, Emily Gregory
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/crucial-conversations-tools-for-talking-when-stakes-are-high/
Core idea: Most problems last because we dodge or botch the talks that matter most, and the way out is to make it safe for everyone to say what they think, starting with your own motives and your own stories.
About the book: Crucial Conversations (third edition, 2022; first published 2002) is a guide to talking when the stakes are high, opinions differ and feelings run strong. Joseph Grenny, Kerry Patterson, Ron McMillan, Al Switzler and Emily Gregory studied people who raise risky topics and keep the respect of others, and turned what they do into skills. The book argues that most chronic problems come from talks we avoid or handle badly. It is for anyone who goes quiet or blows up when it matters most, at work or at home.
Categories: Negotiation, Business & Career
Length: 8 lessons, 20 min
Lessons:
1. Dialogue and the Fool's Choice: Why we go quiet or attack, and what to aim for instead
2. Start with Heart: Ask what you really want, for you, them and the relationship
3. Master My Stories: The story you tell sets your feeling, so retell it
4. Make It Safe: Spot silence and violence, then rebuild safety
5. STATE My Path: Say a hard thing: facts first, then your story
6. Explore Others’ Paths: Help someone who goes silent or gets angry
7. Retake Your Pen: Take tough feedback without being crushed
8. Move to Action: Decide how you decide, then say who does what by when

### Ego Is the Enemy — Ryan Holiday
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/ego-is-the-enemy/
Core idea: Ego is an unhealthy belief in your own importance, and it works against you when you aim for a goal, when you reach it and when you fail. Humility and steady work are the cure.
About the book: Ego Is the Enemy is a 2016 book by Ryan Holiday. He defines ego as an unhealthy belief in our own importance and argues that it works against us at every stage: when we aim for something, when we succeed and when we fail. With stories from history, sports and business, he shows how humility, steady work and purpose can take its place.
Categories: Productivity, Self-Growth
Length: 8 lessons, 19 min
Lessons:
1. Talk less, work more: Why talk feels like progress, and what to do instead.
2. Be something, or do something: A pilot’s fork in the road, and why purpose beats passion.
3. Stay a student: Why a guitarist paid for lessons after joining a famous band.
4. Don’t believe your own story: A coach who refused to say he had planned it all.
5. Success makes ego worse: Entitlement, control and paranoia, and the habit that keeps them away.
6. Know what matters to you: Two generals offered anything: one stayed content, one was ruined.
7. Use failure: What a man in prison did with his time, and how not to make a failure worse.
8. The effort is enough: Judge your work by your own standard, not the scoreboard.

### Good Vibes, Good Life — Vex King
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/good-vibes-good-life/
Core idea: Vex King argues that loving yourself, which means accepting who you are while you keep growing, lifts your mood, and that your mood decides what comes back to you.
About the book: Good Vibes, Good Life (2018) is a self-help book by British writer and mind coach Vex King. King draws on his own hard childhood and on spiritual teachers to argue that loving yourself means accepting who you are while you keep growing, and that your feelings and beliefs shape what comes into your life. He gives habits for mood, relationships, goals and purpose. It is for readers who want a warm, spiritual push, and some of its ideas are beliefs with no scientific proof.
Categories: Self-Growth, Happiness
Length: 8 lessons, 18 min
Lessons:
1. Self-love is two things: Accept who you are and keep growing
2. Your feelings are your vibe: King’s claim: feel good first and good things follow
3. Turn bad feelings around: Five steps instead of burying them
4. Put yourself first: Guard your energy so you can give
5. Compare only with yesterday: Stop measuring your life against other people’s
6. Beliefs steer your life: Change one by finding proof
7. A wish needs action: Write the goal, then take small steps
8. Pain points to purpose: Find the lesson and follow what excites you

### Grit — Angela Duckworth
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/grit/
Core idea: What you achieve over a lifetime depends more on grit than on talent. Grit is passion and perseverance for a goal that matters to you, and it can be grown.
About the book: Grit is a 2016 book by the psychologist Angela Duckworth. She was a math teacher before she studied who sticks with hard things, from West Point cadets to spelling bee finalists. She argues that grit, which means passion and perseverance for long-term goals, matters more than talent, and that anyone can grow it from the inside and with help from other people.
Categories: Self-Growth
Length: 8 lessons, 19 min
Lessons:
1. Effort counts twice: Why talent alone is never enough
2. Passion is a compass: One top goal, held for years
3. Grit can grow: Four parts that build on each other
4. Interest comes first: How a passion is found and grown
5. Practice the hard way: What experts do differently
6. Purpose keeps passion going: Work that matters to other people
7. Hope gets you up again: Fall seven, rise eight
8. Other people grow your grit: Parents, teachers and teams

### Nonviolent Communication — Marshall B. Rosenberg
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/nonviolent-communication/
Core idea: Judging and demanding make people defend themselves or give in out of fear. Saying what you see, feel, need and ask for, and hearing the same four things in others, lets people give from the heart.
About the book: Nonviolent Communication (second edition, 2003) is a guide to talking and listening without blame. Marshall Rosenberg, a psychologist, built it from his work with families, schools, prisons and groups in conflict. It teaches four parts: what you see, what you feel, what you need and what you ask for, and how to hear the same four things in others. It is for anyone who wants fewer fights and closer relationships.
Categories: Negotiation, Self-Growth
Length: 7 lessons, 18 min
Lessons:
1. The four parts: What to say: see, feel, need, ask
2. Describe, don't judge: Why labels start fights, and what to say instead
3. Name what you feel: Real feelings versus hidden opinions
4. Find the need behind it: Why others never cause your feelings, and what to do with anger
5. Ask, don't demand: Make a request someone can say no to
6. Listen for feelings and needs: How to hear someone who is upset or angry
7. Be gentle with yourself: Turn “I should” into the need behind it

### The Four Agreements — Don Miguel Ruiz
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/the-four-agreements/
Core idea: As children we agreed to beliefs we never chose, and four new agreements can replace the ones that make us suffer.
About the book: The Four Agreements is a short 1997 book by Don Miguel Ruiz, who presents it as Toltec wisdom from southern Mexico. It argues that, as children, we agreed to beliefs we never chose, and that these beliefs now shape how we feel and act. It offers four new agreements to replace them, for anyone who wants less self-blame, calmer relationships and more freedom.

3. Don't take anything personally: What others say and do is about them, not about you.
4. Don't make assumptions: Ask instead of guessing, and many fights never start.
5. Always do your best: Your best changes every day. Give that, no more and no less.

### Why Nations Fail — Daron Acemoglu and James A. Robinson
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/why-nations-fail/
Core idea: Nations are rich or poor because of their institutions, the rules that decide who can work, invest and hold power. Rules that share power make a country rich. Rules that let a few take from the many keep it poor.
About the book: Why Nations Fail: The Origins of Power, Prosperity, and Poverty is a 2012 book by the economists Daron Acemoglu and James A. Robinson. Using stories from Nogales, Korea, England, Botswana, Brazil and many other places, it argues that nations are rich or poor because of their institutions, not their climate, culture or leaders' ignorance. Rules that share power and chances bring wealth, and rules that let a few take from the many bring poverty. The summary covers how those rules begin, why rulers block new ideas, how rules protect themselves, and what can change them.
Categories: Society & Tech
Length: 9 lessons, 22 min
Lessons:
1. Three answers that fail: Climate, culture and bad advice do not explain poor countries.
2. Inclusive and extractive rules: Two kinds of rules, and what each does to a country.
3. Power picks the rules: Why politics decides which rules a country gets.
4. Why rulers block new ideas: The fear of creative destruction.
5. Growth that runs out: Why fast growth under a few rulers does not last.
6. Small differences, big moments: How one shock sent two regions down opposite roads.
7. The virtuous circle: How good rules protect themselves.
8. The vicious circle: How bad rules protect themselves too.
9. How countries change: What changes a country, and what does not.

7. Slow your brain waves: What meditation does, and when to do it.
8. Seven steps to a new self: The whole four-week method.

### Getting Things Done — David Allen
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/getting-things-done/
Core idea: Your mind is "for having ideas, not for holding them", so get everything that has your attention out of your head, decide the next step on each thing, and review it all every week.
About the book: Getting Things Done (2001, updated in 2015) is David Allen's guide to staying calm and productive when you have too much to do. Allen is a productivity coach who has taught his method to thousands of people one on one and to hundreds of thousands in seminars. The book argues that stress comes from unfinished things held in your head, and it teaches a five-step habit of capturing, clarifying, organizing, reflecting and engaging. ### Guns, Germs, and Steel — Jared Diamond
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/guns-germs-and-steel/
Core idea: Peoples ended up with different power because of the land, plants and animals they started with, not because of any difference in their minds.
About the book: Guns, Germs, and Steel (1997) is a book by the biologist Jared Diamond. It asks why some peoples ended up with far more power and goods than others, and answers that the cause was geography, not brains. Wild plants and animals, the shape of the continents, the spread of crops, germs from herds and the rise of states made the difference.

5. Tilted axes: Why crops moved fast across Eurasia and slowly elsewhere
6. Germs from herds: Why Europe's diseases killed the Americas, not the reverse
7. Copied inventions: How writing and tools spread, and why geography matters
8. From bands to kings: Why big societies need chiefs and states
9. The test on every continent: The same causes in Australia, Africa and Asia

### Surrounded by Idiots — Thomas Erikson
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/surrounded-by-idiots/
Core idea: In Erikson's model, people act in four main styles, and you get through to anyone by meeting them on their terms, not yours.
About the book: Surrounded by Idiots is a communication book by the Swedish author Thomas Erikson, translated from Swedish. It uses a method called DISC to describe four styles of behavior, which the book calls Red, Yellow, Green and Blue. It argues that people we call idiots are mostly just different, and that you get through to them by adjusting to their style. It is Erikson's model, not settled science, for readers who work or live with people unlike themselves.
Categories: Business & Career, Negotiation, Society & Tech

5. Say hard things well: Giving criticism, and even praise, to each style.
6. How each style loses its temper: Four different ways of getting angry.
7. Build teams from all four: Why a group of one style fails.

### Getting to Yes — Roger Fisher, William Ury, Bruce Patton
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/getting-to-yes/
Core idea: You do not have to choose between being hard and being soft. Settle the problem itself, not a contest of will, protect the person across the table, and look for a result both sides can call fair.
About the book: Getting to Yes is a short guide to negotiating, first published in 1981 by Roger Fisher and William Ury of the Harvard Negotiation Project, with Bruce Patton as editor and later coauthor. It argues that you do not have to choose between being hard and being soft. It offers a method called principled negotiation: settle the problem itself of the problem, look for results that help both sides, and be fair to the people. It is written for anyone who negotiates, from a raise to a peace treaty.

4. Invent options for mutual gain: Make a bigger pile of choices before you decide
5. Insist on objective criteria: Let a fair standard decide, not a contest of will
6. Know your BATNA: Your power is what you can do if there is no deal
7. When they push, don't push back: Turn their attack toward the problem, and spot dirty tricks

About the book: Mastery (2012) is Robert Greene’s guide to how people reach the highest level of skill in any field. Greene, the author of The 48 Laws of Power, studied the lives of great masters such as Leonardo da Vinci, Charles Darwin and Mozart, and interviewed nine living ones. He argues that mastery is not a gift of genius but the result of a long process in three phases, which anyone can follow by choosing the right work and staying with it for years. It is for anyone who wants to build deep skill and a career that fits who they are.

3. Love is giving: Giving shows you are alive, and love has four parts
4. From being loved to loving: How a child grows from being loved to loving
5. Love is not for one person only: Love is one attitude toward everyone

### The Millionaire Next Door — Thomas J. Stanley and William D. Danko
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/the-millionaire-next-door/
Core idea: Most American millionaires are ordinary people who spend far less than they earn and invest the rest, while many high earners who look rich own little.
About the book: The Millionaire Next Door is a 1996 study of how ordinary Americans become wealthy. Thomas J. Stanley and William D. Danko studied millionaires for twenty years. They argue that wealth comes from spending far less than you earn, planning, and raising independent children, not from luck, inheritance or a show of status. It is for anyone who earns well but cannot seem to build wealth.
Categories: Money & Investments
Length: 7 lessons, 17 min
Lessons:
1. Wealth is what you keep: Net worth, not pay, makes you wealthy.
2. Live below your means: Millionaires spend little and invest first.
3. Plan before you spend: Budget, set goals, and give money time each month.
4. Status is a costly treadmill: Showing wealth uses up the money that builds it.
5. Cash gifts hold adults back: The more adult children are given, the less they build.
6. Raise children who stand alone: Independence grows from example and from struggle.
7. Own your work: Most millionaires are self-employed in plain businesses.

### The Selfish Gene — Richard Dawkins
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/the-selfish-gene/
Core idea: Evolution works on genes, not on groups: genes that copy themselves well spread, bodies are the machines they build, and kindness shows up among relatives and between players who meet again.
About the book: The Selfish Gene is a popular science book by the zoologist Richard Dawkins, first published in 1976. It argues that evolution is best seen from the point of view of the gene, the thing that gets copied, and that bodies are machines that carry genes along. It explains why animals help their relatives, raise their young, choose mates and sometimes cooperate, and it adds the idea of the meme. It is for anyone who wants a new way to see why living things act as they do.
Categories: Society & Tech
Length: 9 lessons, 25 min
Lessons:
1. Not for the good of the group: Why a gift to the whole group cannot win
2. Genes and the machines they build: Copies, mistakes and bodies that carry them
3. Genes set rules, brains decide: Why genes build brains instead of steering
4. Hawks, doves and stable strategies: The mix of behavior that nobody can beat
5. Why we help our relatives: How close kin make helping pay
6. Parents and children want different deals: The quiet quarrel over milk and food
7. Mates share children, not interests: Why each partner is tempted to do less
8. How cooperation can win: Nice, forgiving and not envious beats cheating
9. Memes: ideas that copy themselves: A new copier that spreads from mind to mind

Core idea: Spend less than you earn, avoid debt, and put the rest in one low-cost fund that owns the whole stock market. Then stay calm when it falls.
About the book: The Simple Path to Wealth is a plain guide to investing by J.L. Collins, first published in 2016. It grew out of letters he wrote to his teenage daughter, and then his blog. Collins argues that you build wealth by spending less than you earn, avoiding debt, and putting the surplus in a low-cost index fund that owns the whole stock market. He writes for readers who have little time or interest for money.

Core idea: Joseph Nguyen says that events do not make you suffer, your thinking about them does, and when that thinking settles, peace is what is left.
About the book: Don’t Believe Everything You Think (2022) is Joseph Nguyen’s short guide to what he sees as the root of suffering. Nguyen, a coach, argues that events do not hurt us, but our thinking about them does, and that peace is what remains when thinking settles. He builds this on the Three Principles he credits to Sydney Banks, and on simple thought experiments you try on yourself. It is meant for anyone caught in worry, and its claims are one person’s view of the mind, not established science.

### Eat That Frog! — Brian Tracy
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/eat-that-frog/
Core idea: Start each day with your biggest, most important task, and stay on it until it is done.
About the book: Eat That Frog! is a 2007 book (second edition) by Brian Tracy, a speaker and trainer on personal success, about beating procrastination. It gives 21 short ways to choose your most important task, start it and finish it, built on one idea: do your biggest task first each day. It is for anyone with more to do than time.

7. Keep your energy up: Rest, sleep and exercise help you start and finish.

### Games People Play — Eric Berne

Core idea: Much of what people do together is a game: a set of moves with a hidden message that ends in a predictable payoff. Spot the game, and you can stop playing it.
About the book: Games People Play (1964) is a book by the psychiatrist Eric Berne. It argues that much of everyday social life follows hidden patterns he calls games, learned in childhood and repeated for a payoff the players do not admit. It teaches how to spot a game, how to step out of it, and what a life of awareness, spontaneity and intimacy looks like. It is for anyone who wonders why the same fights and routines keep coming back.

6. How to stop a game: Decline the payoff, and what happens next

About the book: Playing to Win (2013) is a guide to strategy by A.G. Lafley, who was chief executive of Procter & Gamble, and Roger L. Martin, a business school dean and strategy adviser. ### Quiet — Susan Cain

Core idea: Our culture treats the bold, talkative style as the best one. Yet up to half of Americans are introverts, and quiet strengths are powers we cannot afford to waste.
About the book: Quiet is a 2012 book by Susan Cain, a former Wall Street lawyer. It argues that our schools, workplaces and culture favor bold, talkative people, even though one third to one half of Americans are introverts. Drawing on psychology and brain research, it explains where introversion comes from and shows how quiet people lead, create and think. About the book: The Laws of Human Nature (2018) is Robert Greene's guide to why people act as they do. About the book: All About Love: New Visions is a 2000 book by the writer and cultural critic bell hooks. Scott Peck and Erich Fromm, she describes love as a choice and an action. She shows how honesty, fairness, community and courage can bring us back to it.

### Capital in the 21st Century — Thomas Piketty
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/capital-in-the-21st-century/
Core idea: When wealth earns more each year than the economy grows, money from the past pulls ahead of pay from the present, and inequality rises unless people choose to act.
About the book: Capital in the Twenty-First Century (2014) is a book by the French economist Thomas Piketty. He gathers income and wealth records from more than twenty countries over three centuries to ask how wealth and income are shared. His central finding is that when the return on capital stays above the growth of the economy, wealth from the past grows faster than pay, and inequality rises. He ends with policy ideas, mainly a yearly tax on wealth that rises with the size of the fortune.
Categories: Money & Investments, Society & Tech
Length: 8 lessons, 21 min
Lessons:
1. Wealth, counted in years of income: What capital is, and how it splits a country's income
2. Slow growth makes wealth heavy: Why the same saving adds up to more in a slow economy
3. When money grows faster than the economy: The rule r > g, and why big fortunes pull ahead
4. Wars, not growth, made us more equal: Why inequality fell last century, and why it is back
5. Wealth is far less equal than pay: Who owns what, and the middle class that owns property
6. Top managers set their own pay: The jump in top salaries since 1980
7. Inheritance is coming back: Balzac's warning, and work against family money
8. A yearly tax on wealth: Piketty's answer, and why banks must share data

About the book: Psycho-Cybernetics (1960) is a self-help classic by Maxwell Maltz, a plastic surgeon. Maltz noticed that a new face did not always change a patient, and he concluded that the picture people hold of themselves, the self-image, sets what they can do. Borrowing ideas from cybernetics, the science of self-steering machines, he describes the brain as a goal-seeking system that you can aim with imagination, relaxation and new habits. It is for anyone held back by doubt, worry or old hurts.

8. Cut out old hurts: Forgive completely, yourself too

About the book: Steve Jobs is the 2011 biography by Walter Isaacson, based on more than forty talks with Jobs over two years and interviews with more than a hundred people who knew him. It follows the Apple co-founder from his adoption and his Silicon Valley childhood through the Mac, his firing, his return, and the iPod, iPhone and iPad. It shows how his love of perfection, simplicity and control made great products, and how his harshness hurt people. It is for anyone who wants lessons about innovation, leadership and character.

7. Show people what they will want: Why he skipped market research and replaced his own hit.

### Tuesdays with Morrie — Mitch Albom

Core idea: A silly question, answered seriously with simple numbers, shows you how the world really works.
About the book: What If? is a collection of answers to the wild questions readers send to Randall Munroe, the former NASA roboticist who draws the stick-figure webcomic xkcd. First published in 2014, it takes each absurd question seriously and answers it with simple math and real data, from a baseball pitched near the speed of light to a hair dryer in a box. It shows a way to think about any big question, for anyone who likes science, numbers and a good joke.
Categories: Society & Tech, Home & Environment
Length: 7 lessons, 19 min
Lessons:

3. Find what really limits you: The hard part is often not the one you first think.
4. Trust the numbers, not your instinct: At extremes, your instincts point at the wrong danger.
5. Make big numbers something you can picture: Match a number to something you have done.
6. Look for the weak link: A neat plan often has one catch.

About the book: Team of Teams (2015) is by retired U.S. Army general Stanley McChrystal with Tantum Collins, David Silverman and Chris Fussell. It tells how an elite special operations Task Force in Iraq was losing to Al Qaeda in Iraq, a weaker but more adaptable network, and how it changed itself to win. It argues that in a fast, tangled world, big organizations must stop chasing efficiency alone and work as a team of teams, with shared information and decisions made close to the problem. It uses stories from war, aviation, medicine, NASA and business.

### The Design of Everyday Things — Don Norman
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/the-design-of-everyday-things/
Core idea: When a thing is hard to use, the design failed, not you. Good design shows what to do, answers every action, and expects people to slip.
About the book: The Design of Everyday Things is a classic about why doors, stoves, taps and screens confuse us. Don Norman, a psychologist and former engineer who also worked at Apple, first wrote it in 1988 and revised it in 2013. He argues that when people struggle, the fault lies in the design, and he lays out principles that make things clear: visible signals, controls that match their results, honest feedback and room for error. It is for anyone who makes things, buys things or has ever pushed a door that should be pulled.
Categories: Society & Tech
Length: 8 lessons, 20 min
Lessons:
1. Blame the design, not yourself: It is not your fault

4. Natural mapping lines up controls: Why you turn on the wrong burner
5. Show how it works and what happened: The story in your head, and feedback
6. Constraints make wrong moves hard: Let only the right move fit
7. Design for the slip: Why experts slip, and how design helps
8. Solve the right problem: Watch people, test, repeat

About the book: The Lean Startup (2011) by Eric Ries argues that a new business is an experiment. He shows how to test an idea cheaply with a rough first version, measure real progress, and know when to change course. The book grew out of his own failed first company and his work at IMVU, and it borrows ideas from Toyota’s lean factories. It is for founders and for people who build new products inside large companies.

### Turn the Ship Around! — L. David Marquet
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/turn-the-ship-around/
Core idea: In Marquet's account, people treated as followers act like followers; give them control, plus the competence and the clarity to use it, and they act like leaders.
About the book: Turn the Ship Around! is a leadership book by L. David Marquet, a US Navy officer who commanded the nuclear submarine USS Santa Fe from 1999 to 2001. It tells how he took over a crew at the bottom of the fleet and, within a year, turned it into one of the best. He argues that people treated as followers act like followers, so a leader should give control away while building people's competence and their understanding of the goal. It is written for bosses and teams in any workplace.

6. Learn, don't just be briefed: Quiz the team instead of talking at it.
7. Aim for excellence, not for avoiding errors: Give people a goal and principles they can decide with.
8. Emancipate, don't just empower: Release talent, and what lasts after the leader leaves.

### A People's History of the United States — Howard Zinn
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/a-people-s-history-of-the-united-states/
Core idea: Told from below, American history shows a few powerful people using the nation, the law and war to protect their wealth, and ordinary people who pushed back again and again and sometimes won.
About the book: A People's History of the United States, first published in 1980, is Howard Zinn's account of American history from Columbus to the early 2000s. He tells it from the side of Native Americans, enslaved people, workers, women and soldiers, not only presidents and generals. Zinn, a historian who took part in the civil rights and anti-war movements, argues that governments serve the powerful, and that ordinary people have changed the country by resisting.
Categories: Society & Tech
Length: 8 lessons, 24 min
Lessons:
1. Whose side tells the story: A history that follows the leaders hides the people they hurt
2. How the color line began: Racism grew from conditions, and rulers kept poor people apart
3. A revolution for whom: Leaders used the people's anger, then fenced it in
4. Land taken, promises broken: Indian removal opened land for profit through broken treaties
5. Freedom pushed from below: Leaders moved only as the pressure grew
6. Force first, then a little help: Strikes met troops, then small gains kept the system standing
7. War and the state: Wars serve the powerful, and war silences dissent
8. Ordinary people can win: Change came from people acting together

### A Room of One's Own — Virginia Woolf
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/a-room-of-ones-own/
Core idea: A woman needs money of her own and a room with a lock on the door if she is to write fiction, because a free mind needs both, and for centuries women had neither.
About the book: A Room of One's Own is a long essay by the English writer Virginia Woolf, written from two talks she gave in October 1928 to student societies at Newnham and Girton colleges. Through the story of a made-up speaker, it argues that a woman needs money of her own and a room with a lock on the door if she is to write fiction. It looks at why women had neither, and at what poverty, anger and a lack of earlier women writers did to the work of women before the 1900s. It is for anyone who wants to know what a writer needs besides talent.
Categories: Self-Growth, Society & Tech
Length: 7 lessons, 18 min
Lessons:
1. Money and a lock on the door: What a steady income and a private room give a mind
2. Where the money went: Why women's colleges and mothers had none to give
3. Why the professors were angry: What loud opinions about women really protect
4. Shakespeare's sister: Why a woman with his gift could not have used it
5. A mind with nothing in the way: How anger and grievance bend a writer's work
6. We think back through our mothers: Why writers need those who wrote before them
7. The lives nobody wrote: What books left out about women

### Elon Musk — Ashlee Vance

Core idea: Elon Musk builds companies to solve problems he has cared about since he was young, and he gets there by learning fast, risking his own money and asking for the impossible.
About the book: Elon Musk and the Quest for a Fantastic Future is the young readers’ edition (2017) of Ashlee Vance’s biography of Musk. Vance is a technology reporter who talked to about two hundred people who knew Musk before Musk agreed to help. The book follows Musk from a lonely boyhood in South Africa to Zip2, PayPal, SpaceX, Tesla and SolarCity, and its story stops in 2016. It argues that Musk builds companies to solve problems he has cared about since youth, such as clean energy and a second home for people, and that his way of working has a real human cost.

Lessons:
1. A mission bigger than money: Why Musk picks goals that could change the world.
2. Learn it yourself: How he studies a new field until he can plan the work.
3. Ask what it should cost: Why SpaceX and Tesla make so much themselves.
4. Put your own money on the line: What he risked, and how close he came to losing it.
5. Fail, fix, fly again: How four launches taught SpaceX to reach orbit.
6. Keep hold of the vision: Why he fights to stay in charge.

### Emotional Blackmail — Susan Forward with Donna Frazier
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/emotional-blackmail/
Core idea: Emotional blackmail is a threat from someone close: do what I want, or you will suffer. It works through fear, obligation and guilt, and it ends when you change how you respond.
About the book: Emotional Blackmail is a self-help book by the therapist Susan Forward, written with Donna Frazier and first published in 1997. It shows how people close to us use fear, obligation and guilt to make us give in, and why both sides play their parts. Its second half teaches step-by-step ways to answer pressure calmly and to stand by your own choices. It is for anyone who keeps giving in to a partner, parent, boss or friend.

6. Stop, observe, decide: What to do before you answer
7. Say it without defending: Four ways to hold your ground

### Factfulness — Hans Rosling, Ola Rosling and Anna Rosling Rönnlund
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/factfulness-ten-reasons-we-re-wrong-about-the-world/
Core idea: Almost everyone sees the world as more frightening and hopeless than it is, because ten built-in instincts pull our thinking toward drama.
About the book: Factfulness is a 2018 book by the Swedish doctor and professor Hans Rosling with his son Ola Rosling and his daughter-in-law Anna Rosling Rönnlund. Hans Rosling tested thousands of people with simple fact questions about the world and found that most score worse than chimpanzees guessing at random. The book says ten built-in instincts pull us toward a more dramatic, frightening view than the data show, and gives a simple rule for controlling each one.

5. Compare and divide: How to put a lonely number in proportion
6. Question your categories: Income shapes life more than culture does
7. Look for causes, not villains: Why blaming one person stops you thinking
8. Take a breath: Now or never is almost never true

Core idea: People respond to incentives, and when you follow the data, the popular story is often wrong.
About the book: Freakonomics is a 2005 book, revised in 2006, by the economist Steven D. Levitt and the writer Stephen J. Dubner. It uses data to answer odd questions, from why teachers cheat to why drug dealers live with their moms. It argues that incentives drive what people do, that the popular story is often wrong, and that the cause of a big change can be far away.

6. Correlation is not cause: Two things can move together for other reasons

Core idea: Bezos built Amazon by thinking in years, serving customers instead of rivals, and inventing through many bold bets, and he tried to keep it Day One as the company grew.
About the book: Invent & Wander (2021) collects the writings of Jeff Bezos: his yearly letters to Amazon’s shareholders from 1997 to 2019, plus talks and interviews, with an introduction by the biographer Walter Isaacson. Bezos argues for thinking in years, putting customers ahead of rivals, making bold bets and accepting many failures, and keeping the energy of a young company, which he calls Day One. ### On Writing — Stephen King
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/on-writing/
Core idea: Writing is one mind reaching another, and hard work can make a competent writer good: read a lot, write a lot, use plain honest words, find the story, and cut your second draft.
About the book: On Writing (2000) is Stephen King's short book about the craft of writing fiction. It is part memoir, telling how King became a writer, and part guide, with the tools and habits he uses. King argues that a competent writer can become a good one by reading a lot, writing a lot, using plain and honest words, finding stories instead of plotting them, and rewriting with care. It is for anyone who wants to write better, whether or not they like horror.
Categories: Productivity, Personalities
Length: 8 lessons, 18 min
Lessons:
1. What shaped a writer: A mother's push, a pile of rejections, an editor's pen and a wife's belief
2. Writing is telepathy: A few true details, and the reader finishes the picture
3. The toolbox: Plain words, active verbs and few adverbs
4. Read a lot, write a lot: The two things King says you must do
5. A door you shut: A room, a word goal and a first draft written alone
6. A situation, not a plot: Dig the story up instead of building it
7. Rewrite with the door open: Rest the draft, cut a tenth, ask a trusted reader
8. Write for the joy of it: Why King writes, and how it helped him after an accident

He asks why a man who spent his life on the move found some of his deepest joy in sitting still, and he tells what he learned from a Zen center, a monk who used to be a scientist, and busy companies. ### The Fire Next Time — James Baldwin
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/the-fire-next-time/
Core idea: James Baldwin says America's race problem grows out of white fear and white innocence, that hating back harms the hater too, and that Black and white Americans can only be free together.
About the book: The Fire Next Time (1963) is James Baldwin's pair of essays on race, faith and love in America. Baldwin, a Black writer from Harlem, writes a letter to his young nephew and then looks back on his boyhood, his years as a young preacher and a dinner with the leader of the Nation of Islam. He argues that white fear and innocence sit at the root of racism, that hating back harms the hater too, and that Black and white Americans can only be free together. It is one man's view, for anyone who wants to understand it.

5. Accept the past, then use it: Why a made-up past always fails
6. Free together: Why white freedom depends on Black freedom
7. The fire next time: The warning in the title, and the choice

### The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks — Rebecca Skloot
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/the-immortal-life-of-henrietta-lacks/
Core idea: In 1951 doctors took cells from a poor Black woman without telling her, and those cells became one of the most useful tools in medicine, while her family was never told.
About the book: The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks is a 2010 nonfiction book by the science writer Rebecca Skloot. It tells how cells taken in 1951 from Henrietta Lacks, a poor Black mother of five, became the first human cells to keep dividing in a lab without end. It follows the science, the history of research ethics and the Lacks family, above all Henrietta’s daughter Deborah, who spent her life trying to learn who her mother was. It is for anyone who wants to know whose body medicine rests on.
Categories: Health, Personalities
Length: 7 lessons, 20 min
Lessons:
1. The woman behind the letters: Who Henrietta was, and how a piece of her tumor was taken
2. Cells that would not die: Why her cells kept dividing when all the others died
3. A workhorse for the world: How the cells helped test a polio vaccine, then spread everywhere
4. Taking without asking: How one doctor’s secret shots led to rules about consent
5. Why trust was broken: The history behind the Lacks family’s fear of hospitals
6. A family nobody told: How the family found out, and what they wanted
7. Who owns your tissue: What the law says about cells once they leave your body

### The Man Who Mistook His Wife for a Hat — Oliver Sacks
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/the-man-who-mistook-his-wife-for-a-hat/
Core idea: A brain illness is never only something taken away: the person inside keeps working to stay themselves, so to understand a patient you need their story, not just a list of what is wrong.
About the book: The Man Who Mistook His Wife for a Hat is a 1985 book by Oliver Sacks, a British neurologist. It tells 24 true stories about patients whose brains lost a skill, had too much of one, or played back the past. Sacks argues that to understand an illness you must know the person, because a patient is always working to stay themselves. It is for anyone curious about the brain and what makes us who we are.

Length: 7 lessons, 20 min
Lessons:
1. Seeing the parts, missing the person: A man who knew every feature and no face
2. A self is a story: Two men with no memory, and what is left
3. The hidden sense of your body: A woman who lost it and felt disembodied
4. Patients invent their own fixes: Glasses with a level, a spinning chair, hands that learn
5. When too much feels like health: Too much energy can be a gift and a trap
6. The brain keeps your past: The same replay means different things to different people
7. Look past the gaps: What holds a mind together when puzzles fail

### The Sum of Us — Heather McGhee
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/the-sum-of-us/
Core idea: The belief that one group gains only when another loses is a false story, and it has drained the shared goods that most Americans depend on.
About the book: The Sum of Us (2021) by Heather McGhee asks why Americans cannot have nice things such as good schools, health care and fair pay. After years in economic policy, she traveled the country and found that a false zero-sum story, in which one race's gain is another's loss, has drained shared goods for almost everyone. Through stories from a drained pool to a Mississippi car plant and a Maine mill town, she shows what racism costs all Americans and what people can win when they join together.
Categories: Society & Tech
Length: 8 lessons, 20 min
Lessons:
1. The zero-sum story: Why one group’s gain was told as another’s loss.
2. Racism drained the pool: How a public pool, college and health care were lost.
3. The canary in the coal mine: How risky loans spread from the first victims to all.
4. Divided workers win less: How splitting workers keeps pay low, and how they win.
5. A democracy with holes: How voting rules built for some caught many.
6. The same sky: Why pollution and costs reach everyone.
7. The hidden wound: What denial and fear cost white Americans.
8. The Solidarity Dividend: What people win together, and how to aim for it.

Core idea: Abuse comes from a man's attitudes of ownership and entitlement, not from his feelings, so a partner cannot fix him by understanding him or by being easier to live with.
About the book: Why Does He Do That? is a 2002 guide by Lundy Bancroft, who counseled abusive men for about fifteen years. It explains the thinking behind angry and controlling behavior by a partner, from the first warning signs to what real change takes. It is written mainly for women who are mistreated by a partner, and for friends and professionals who want to help.

### Surely You’re Joking, Mr. Feynman! — Richard P. Feynman
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/surely-youre-joking-mr-feynman/
Core idea: Real understanding is something you test for yourself, with puzzles, plain examples, play and honesty, never with names, titles or the word of experts.
About the book: Surely You’re Joking, Mr. Feynman! is a book of true stories by the physicist Richard Feynman, collected by his drumming friend Ralph Leighton and first published in 1985. It follows Feynman from fixing radios as a boy to the atomic bomb project, teaching in Brazil and a Nobel Prize. The stories are funny, and together they show a mind that tests everything for itself. It is for anyone who likes curious people, science or learning.
Categories: Personalities, Self-Growth

3. Hold one example in your head: Ask for one real case, and ask early.
4. Talk to the idea, not the person: Fame in the room did not change what he said about the physics.
5. Play first, importance later: A wobbling plate led to the work behind a Nobel Prize.
6. Do not fool yourself: The easiest person to fool is you.
7. Look at the thing itself: He read every book himself, and one with nothing in it still had a rating.
8. Be a beginner in the open: Be bad first, practice, and stop minding.

### Ikigai — Héctor García, Francesc Miralles
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/ikigai/
Core idea: A long, happy life starts with a reason to get up each morning, kept alive by staying busy, close to friends, light on food, gentle in movement and calm in pace.
About the book: Ikigai is a short book by Héctor García and Francesc Miralles, first published in Spanish in 2016. The authors visited Ogimi, a village on the island of Okinawa where people live longer than almost anywhere, and interviewed its oldest residents. They argue that a reason to get up each morning, kept alive by friends, light food, gentle movement and a calm pace, is the Japanese secret to a long and happy life. It is for anyone who wants more meaning and energy in everyday life.
Categories: Happiness
Length: 7 lessons, 18 min
Lessons:
1. A reason to get up: What ikigai is, and why Japan has no word for retiring
2. Meaning is found, not made: Viktor Frankl on discovering your purpose
3. Lose yourself in the doing: Flow: a stretch, a clear aim and one task at a time
4. Stay close to your people: The moai, a group that looks after its members
5. Eat light, move often: Stop at 80 percent full, and keep moving all day
6. Busy, but never in a rush: Stress wears the body down, a small challenge helps
7. Fall seven times, rise eight: Setbacks, and how to grow stronger from them

### The Courage to Be Disliked — Ichiro Kishimi, Fumitake Koga
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/the-courage-to-be-disliked/
Core idea: People are not stuck because of their past. They are stuck because change feels scary, and the way out is the courage to live your own life, even if some people dislike you.
About the book: The Courage to Be Disliked is a book by the philosopher Ichiro Kishimi and the writer Fumitake Koga, first published in Japan in 2013. It is a conversation over five nights between a philosopher and a doubtful young man, and it retells the ideas of the psychiatrist Alfred Adler. It argues that people can change at any moment, that the past does not decide who you are, and that happiness comes from feeling of use to others while living your own life, even if some people dislike you.

4. Separate your tasks: Do your part and leave other people's parts to them
5. Freedom costs being disliked: You cannot be free and liked by everyone
6. Equal, never above or below: Skip praise and scolding, and say thank you
7. Happiness is feeling useful: Three things that build a sense of being of use
8. Live each moment like a dance: Give your full effort to now, not to a far summit

### Man’s Search for Meaning — Viktor E. Frankl
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/man-s-search-for-meaning/
Core idea: People are driven most by a search for meaning, not by pleasure or power, and a person with a reason to live can bear almost any hardship, because one freedom can never be taken away: the freedom to choose how to respond.
About the book: Man’s Search for Meaning (first published in German in 1946) is Viktor Frankl’s account of three years in Nazi concentration camps and of the method he built from them. Frankl, a psychiatrist in Vienna, argues that people are driven most by a search for meaning, and that a person with a reason to live can bear almost any hardship. The second part explains his method, logotherapy, and why happiness cannot be chased. It is for anyone who wants to understand what keeps a person going in a hard time.

5. The last freedom: What nobody can take from you
6. Meaning in suffering: What to do with pain you cannot avoid
7. Happiness is a side effect: Why chasing it makes it run away

### The Intelligent Investor — Benjamin Graham, Jason Zweig
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/the-intelligent-investor/
Core idea: Treat a stock as a small piece of a real business: pay less than it is worth, plan for being wrong, and do not let the market’s moods or your own run your money.
About the book: The Intelligent Investor is a classic guide to investing for ordinary people, first published in 1949 by Benjamin Graham, with fresh commentary by Jason Zweig. It teaches that a stock is a share of a real business, that you should pay less than it is worth, and that your own behavior is the biggest risk. It is written for people who want safe, steady results, not quick riches.
Categories: Money & Investments
Length: 7 lessons, 19 min
Lessons:
1. Investing is not speculating: An investor studies a business. A speculator bets on a price.
2. Treat a stock as a business: Ask what it is worth and how much you are paying.
3. Mr. Market: The market names a price every day. You need not accept it.
4. The margin of safety: Pay well under what a thing is worth, so a mistake cannot ruin you.
5. Choose your role and split your money: Most people should be defensive investors with a simple plan.
6. Do not chase the hot streak: Over the long run most funds do worse than the market. Costs and fading streaks are why.
7. Your own worst enemy: How you act matters more than what you own.

### A Brief History of Time — Stephen Hawking

Core idea: The universe runs on laws we can understand, and joining the science of the very big with the science of the very small may show how it all began.
About the book: A Brief History of Time (1988) is Stephen Hawking's tour of the universe for general readers. Hawking, a Cambridge physicist, explains how scientists decide what to believe, how space and time bend, why the universe began with a big bang, how black holes glow, and what time is. He argues that the universe follows laws we can understand, and he describes the hunt for one theory that joins them all.

### As a Man Thinketh — James Allen

About the book: As a Man Thinketh is a short 1902 classic by the British writer James Allen. It argues that your thoughts grow into your character, your circumstances and your health. Allen says you cannot pick your circumstances, but you can pick your thoughts, and that is how you change your life. It is written for any reader who wants more control over their own mind.

### The Bhagavad Gita — Vyasa
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/the-bhagavad-gita/
Core idea: You are a deathless self, so do your duty with a steady mind, let go of the reward, and make God your refuge.
About the book: The Bhagavad Gita is an old Sanskrit poem from India, set inside the epic Mahabharata. In it, Krishna, who is God in the poem, talks with the prince Arjuna in a war chariot between two armies. They speak of the deathless self, duty without hunger for reward, a steady mind and devotion. This summary follows Sir Edwin Arnold's English translation, for any reader who wants to know what the poem teaches.
Categories: Spirituality, Self-Growth
Length: 7 lessons, 17 min
Lessons:
1. You are more than your body: The self never dies, so grief over what passes is a mistake.

About the book: Talking to Strangers (2019) is Malcolm Gladwell’s look at why we so often misjudge people we do not know. Gladwell, a staff writer at The New Yorker and a bestselling author, builds the book on true cases: a spy in the Pentagon, an investment fraud, a prime minister and Hitler, and a traffic stop that ended in a death. He argues that we start by believing strangers, read their faces as if they showed feelings, and ignore the setting a person is in. It is for anyone who has to judge people they have just met.

4. Faces are not windows: Feelings do not show on the face the way TV teaches.
5. People who do not match: Honest people who look like liars, and liars who look honest.
6. Behavior has a place: People act in ways that belong to a setting, so look at the setting.

### The Power of Now — Eckhart Tolle
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/the-power-of-now/
Core idea: You are not your mind. The endless thinking in your head, and the old pain it feeds on, cause most of your suffering, and you end it by watching them and giving this moment your full attention.
About the book: The Power of Now (1997) is Eckhart Tolle's guide to ending suffering by living in the present. Tolle, a German-born writer, says he lived in anxiety until a night at 29 when his mind went quiet. The book argues that the endless thinking in your head, and the old pain it feeds on, cause most unhappiness, and that you can step out by watching your thoughts, feeling your body and accepting this moment. It is for anyone tired of worry, regret and inner noise.
Categories: Self-Growth, Happiness

Lessons:

2. Old pain wakes up: Old emotional pain, and how watching it takes its power
3. Now is all there is: Past and future live only as thoughts

5. Feel your inner body: A way into stillness, through the life in your body
6. Relationships are practice: Why love turns to conflict, and what to do

### Why We Sleep — Matthew Walker
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/why-we-sleep/
Core idea: Sleep is not one favor but many: each night it saves your memories, calms your feelings and protects your body, and Walker says we are losing too much of it.
About the book: Why We Sleep is a 2017 book by Matthew Walker, a brain scientist at the University of California, Berkeley. It argues that sleep is not wasted time but a nightly repair job for the brain and body, and that modern life steals too much of it. Walker explains how sleep works, what it does for memory, mood and health, and how to protect it. Some of its health claims have been challenged since it came out.
Categories: Health
Length: 7 lessons, 18 min
Lessons:
1. Two clocks tell you when to sleep: A body clock and a chemical decide when you feel sleepy
2. Two kinds of sleep take turns: Deep sleep comes early, dream sleep comes late
3. Sleep saves what you learn: Sleep readies your brain, then locks in what you learned
4. Short sleep dulls you quietly: A little less sleep wears down attention, quietly
5. Sleep holds up your body: Heart, blood sugar, hunger and your body's defenses
6. Dream sleep resets your feelings: You keep the memory and lose some of its sting
7. How to protect your sleep: Light, drinks, a cool room and Walker's twelve tips

Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/lives-of-the-stoics/
Core idea: The Stoics were judged by what they did, not what they said, and their lives and deaths show how to live well: with four virtues, a calm focus on what you control, and daily practice.
About the book: Lives of the Stoics (2020) tells the stories of 26 Stoics, from Zeno of Kition in the fourth century BC to the Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius. Ryan Holiday and Stephen Hanselman, the authors of The Daily Stoic, say the lives teach as much as the philosophers' own writing. The book shows what Stoicism asks of a person: four virtues, a steady focus on what you control, service to others, and practice for hard times and for death. It is for anyone who wants a philosophy they can use, and it is honest about where its heroes fell short.
Categories: Productivity, Happiness
