4. Doing right costs something: Honest people paid a high price and kept their character
5. You owe other people: Use what you have for the common good
6. Progress, not perfection: Even great minds fell short, and the trying counts
7. Get ready for the blow: Train in calm times for hard days and for death

Core idea: BJ Fogg says that failing to change is a design flaw, not a flaw in you: pick a tiny behavior you already want, tie it to something you already do, and celebrate it right away.
About the book: Tiny Habits (2019) is a book by BJ Fogg, who founded the Behavior Design Lab at Stanford University. He argues that failing to change is a design flaw, not a flaw in you. His method starts with tiny behaviors you already want, ties each one to something you already do, and uses a quick celebration to make it stick. It also shows how to untangle a bad habit, for anyone who wants lasting change.
Categories: Self-Growth, Productivity
Length: 7 lessons, 19 min
Lessons:
1. Three things make a behavior: Motivation, ability and a prompt must meet at the same moment
2. Pick what you already want: Choose behaviors you want to do, not ones you think you should
3. Make it tiny: Shrink a habit until it is easy to do on your worst day
4. The Tiny Habits recipe: After something you already do, do your tiny habit, then celebrate
5. Celebrate to wire it in: A good feeling right after the habit is what makes it stick
6. From tiny to big: Small wins grow into bigger habits and a new view of yourself
7. Untangle a bad habit: Go knot by knot: remove the prompt, make it harder, then swap it

### Declutter Your Mind — S. J. Scott, Barrie Davenport

Core idea: You cannot stop thoughts from coming, but you can learn to watch them, answer them, and clear what feeds them.
About the book: Declutter Your Mind (2016) is a guide by habit writer S. J. Scott and personal coach Barrie Davenport. It argues that stress, too many choices, too much stuff and a brain that leans negative fill your head with noise, and that small daily habits can quiet it. The habits cover your thoughts, your life obligations, your relationships and your surroundings. It is for readers who overthink and want a calmer, simpler mind.

3. Talk back to your thoughts: Name them, test them, accept what is true
4. Know what matters: Values, priorities and three-month goals
5. Clear the people clutter: Be present, forgive, and let go when you must
6. Clear your space and your day: Ten minutes a day, an hour off screens, three goals
7. Live in the present: Full attention for eating, walking, even dishes

Nicholas Boothman, a former fashion and advertising photographer who trained in Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP), argues that you can build rapport, a feeling of common ground, in about a minute and a half. He teaches four skills: your attitude, matching the other person's body and voice, easy conversation, and noticing which sense a person favors. It is written for anyone who wants to feel at ease with strangers, at work and in daily life.

About the book: Nexus (2024) is Yuval Noah Harari's history of information networks, from the stories of Stone Age bands to artificial intelligence. Harari, a historian, argues that information mainly connects people instead of showing the truth, so every network must balance truth with order and needs ways to fix its own mistakes. He uses witch hunts, science, democracy and dictatorship to show how, and asks what changes when AI becomes the first member of the network that is not human. It is for readers who want a long view of today's information problems.

### Sapiens — Yuval Noah Harari
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/sapiens/
Core idea: Humans rule the world because we can believe in shared stories, and those stories let millions of strangers work together.
About the book: Sapiens is a history of our species by the Israeli historian Yuval Noah Harari, first published in Hebrew in 2011 and in English in 2014. It follows humans from 70,000 years ago to today in four parts: the Cognitive Revolution, the Agricultural Revolution, the unification of humankind and the Scientific Revolution, and asks what we will become. Harari argues that shared stories, such as gods, money, nations and companies, let strangers cooperate, and that this power has not clearly made people happier. It is for readers who want the big picture of human history.
Categories: Society & Tech
Length: 10 lessons, 25 min
Lessons:
1. Stories strangers share: Why shared stories, not strength, let us rule the world
2. The giants that vanished: Where Sapiens settled new lands, most big animals soon died out
3. The farming trap: Farming fed more people, but most lives got harder
4. Imagined orders: Laws and classes are shared beliefs, and they still work
5. Money is trust: Why a shell or a piece of paper can buy bread
6. One world: How money, empires and religions joined people together
7. Admitting ignorance: How saying "we do not know" gave us power
8. Trust in the future: Why credit makes the economy grow
9. Power and happiness: We gained power, but not clearly more joy
10. The end of Sapiens: Science may soon replace natural selection with design

Core idea: You cannot control what happens, only what you think and do, so judge calmly, treat people kindly and do your work now.
About the book: Meditations is the private notebook of Marcus Aurelius, Roman emperor from 161 to 180 AD. He wrote it to himself and never meant it to be read by others. It is one of the main surviving books of Stoicism, an old philosophy that says happiness comes from self-control and a calm mind. It has no plot, but a few ideas return again and again: what is in your power, how short life is, and how to treat other people.

4. Meet people with patience: People who wrong you do not know better.

6. Let go of praise: Fame fades fast. Care about what you do.
7. Start the work today: Do the next right thing, not tomorrow.

Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/the-art-of-war/
Core idea: The best win costs the least: you prepare, you learn what the enemy will do, and you win before the fight starts, or without a fight at all.
About the book: The Art of War is a short book on war from ancient China, written by Sun Tzu, a general of the state of Wu who tradition says lived about 2,500 years ago. Its thirteen chapters explain how to plan, how to read the enemy and how to win at the lowest cost. The book's main claim is that the best victory comes from preparing well and knowing more than the enemy, so the fight is won before it starts, or never has to happen. It is for anyone who faces a rival or leads other people. The English text is Lionel Giles's translation.
Categories: Negotiation, Society & Tech, Leadership
Length: 8 lessons, 18 min
Lessons:
1. Count the odds first: Most battles are decided before they start
2. Win without a fight: A long war costs more than it wins
3. Make yourself safe first: Your safety is in your hands, the win is not
4. Know the enemy and yourself: Learn what the enemy will do from people
5. Hit where they are weak: Avoid what is strong, and flow like water
6. Use deception: Let the enemy see what is not true
7. Care and firm rules: People follow a leader who is kind and firm
8. Fight only when it pays: Never go to war out of anger

About the book: The Pomodoro Technique, in its 2018 edition, presents a method Francesco Cirillo began as a university student in the late 1980s and developed by 1992. He teaches a simple routine: work in 25-minute boxes timed by a kitchen timer, rest between them, and count what you finish. The book shows how to handle interruptions, guess effort, keep a steady pace and use the same routine on a team. It is for anyone who wants to focus better and stop fighting the clock.

5. Don't race the clock: Measure how you work instead of judging it

2. Fair means fairly gained: Why how wealth arrives matters more than how it is spread
3. Taxing work, owning people: The self-ownership argument and the replies to it
4. Following the idea to its edge: Selling a kidney, assisted dying and agreed harm

### What money shouldn't buy — Bookmuse
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/justice-5-what-money-cant-buy/
Core idea: Letting money decide can go wrong in two ways: the choice may not be free, and the thing sold may lose its meaning.
About the book: Part 5 of 10 in Justice, our own course on the big ideas of moral and political philosophy. It sets out the case for letting markets decide, then two doubts: a choice made from need is not fully free, and some goods lose their meaning when sold. It builds on Part 4's idea that willing deals are just.
Categories: Society & Tech
Length: 4 lessons, 13 min
Lessons:
1. The case for letting money decide: Why a willing deal looks fair
2. When need makes the choice: The first doubt: is the choice free?
3. Some things change when sold: The second doubt: a price can spoil a good
4. Two doubts that come apart: Why a fairer market can still be wrong

### Duty and motive — Bookmuse
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/justice-6-duty-and-motive/
Core idea: For Kant, an act is good when you do it because it is right, and acting on that reason is what it means to be free.
About the book: Part 6 of 10 in Justice, our own course on the big ideas of moral and political philosophy. It follows Immanuel Kant's view that an act is good because of the reason behind it, and that freedom means acting on a law you give yourself. It builds on Part 2, where utilitarians judged acts by their results.
Categories: Society & Tech
Length: 5 lessons, 14 min
Lessons:
1. Right act, wrong reason: Why the motive gives an act its worth
2. Freedom is not doing what you want: Acting on a law you give yourself
3. Two kinds of should: A command with an “if” and one without
4. The test of everyone: Could you want your rule for all?
5. People are not tools: Treat a person as an end, never merely a means

### Is lying ever right? — Bookmuse
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/justice-7-is-lying-ever-right/
Core idea: Kant says a lie is wrong even to a murderer at the door, a defender finds a line between a lie and a misleading truth, and Kant tests a just law by an agreement that never happened.
About the book: Part 7 of 10 in Justice, our own course on the big ideas of moral and political philosophy. It tests Immanuel Kant's view that you may never lie, even to a murderer at the door, asks whether a lie differs from a misleading truth, and shows how Kant builds justice on an imagined agreement. It builds on Part 6, Kant's test that a moral rule must hold for everyone.
Categories: Society & Tech
Length: 5 lessons, 13 min
Lessons:
1. The murderer at the door: Is a lie ever allowed to save a life?
2. Why a lie fails the test: A rule of lying cannot be a law for all
3. A lie and a true dodge: A line between false and misleading
4. Does the line matter?: The defender's case and its critics
5. Justice from an imagined agreement: A law is just if all could agree to it

### Behind the veil — Bookmuse
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/justice-8-behind-the-veil/
Core idea: The fair rules for a society are the ones we would pick if we did not know where we would end up in it.
About the book: Part 8 of 10 in Justice, our own course on the big ideas of moral and political philosophy. It follows John Rawls, who argued that fair rules are the ones people would choose behind a veil that hides who they will be. It builds on Kant's idea of an imagined agreement from Part 7 and answers the happiness and free-market ideas of Parts 2 and 4.
Categories: Society & Tech
Length: 5 lessons, 14 min
Lessons:
1. When a deal is not fair: Why agreeing is not enough
2. The veil of ignorance: Choosing rules without knowing your place
3. Two rules we would choose: Equal freedoms, and gaps that help the poorest
4. Luck is not earned: Birth and talent are nobody's doing
5. Two objections: Incentives and effort

### Who deserves what — Bookmuse
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/justice-9-who-deserves-what/
Core idea: Who deserves a place or a prize depends on what the thing is for, so arguments about fairness turn into arguments about purpose and honor.
About the book: Part 9 of 10 in Justice, our own course on the big ideas of moral and political philosophy. It asks who deserves what, through the arguments over college admissions and Aristotle's idea that fair shares depend on what a thing is for. It builds on Part 8, where Rawls argues that talent and luck are not deserved.
Categories: Society & Tech
Length: 5 lessons, 14 min
Lessons:
1. Ask what it is for: Aristotle: the purpose comes first
2. Three reasons for a preference: Admissions: tests, past wrongs, diversity
3. The purpose sets the merit: Dworkin's answer, and where it stops
4. Fairness also honors: Why a change of rule can feel like an insult
5. Politics is for becoming good: Aristotle on habit, judgment and who should lead

### What we owe each other — Bookmuse
Page: https://bookmuse.wanngo.com/summaries/justice-10-what-we-owe-each-other/
Core idea: On the view this part ends with, we may owe each other more than we ever agreed to, and a fair society cannot avoid asking what a good life together is.
About the book: Part 10 of 10 in Justice, our own course on the big ideas of moral and political philosophy. It asks whether we owe each other more than we have chosen: duties of membership, the story we are part of, and why a fair society cannot stay neutral about the good life. It builds on Kant's autonomy (Part 6), Rawls's veil (Part 8) and Aristotle's purpose (Part 9).
Categories: Society & Tech
Length: 5 lessons, 14 min
Lessons:
1. Debts we never signed: The idea that we owe only what we choose
2. A third kind of duty: Duties of membership, with no yes needed
3. The story you are part of: Why a life is more than a list of choices
4. Why neutrality runs out: Rules still say what things are for
5. A politics of the common good: Shared places and honest argument
